elements.text: Activation of one or more chemical oxygen generators in the forward cargo compartment initiated the fire.
Loss of control resulting from flight control failure due to extreme heat and structural collapse.
Improper maintenance activities and false entries by SabreTech mechanics regarding the removal of chemical oxygen generators.
Failure to install safety caps on the unexpended chemical oxygen generators.
Lack of a formal system in SabreTech’s shipping and receiving department for tracking hazardous materials.
Failure of SabreTech to properly prepare, package, and identify the unexpended chemical oxygen generators.
ValuJet’s failure to adequately oversee SabreTech’s maintenance operations.
FAA’s inadequate oversight of ValuJet’s maintenance functions and limited oversight capabilities.
Absence of an explicit requirement for the principal maintenance inspector to regularly inspect Part 145 repair stations performing heavy maintenance.
Inadequate inspector resources in the Atlanta FSDO due to rigid application of staffing level models.
Inability of the principal maintenance inspector to provide effective oversight due to excessive workload.
Flightcrew was properly certificated and trained.
No evidence of preexisting medical conditions affecting flightcrew performance.
Flight attendants completed approved training.
Weather was not a factor.
Airplane was equipped and maintained in accordance with regulations with no preexisting mechanical malfunctions.
Ramp agents’ and flightcrew’s acceptance of the shipment was not unreasonable.
ValuJet’s failure to secure the cargo was not unreasonable.
Only a small amount of smoke entered the cockpit before the last recorded verbalization.
Current minimum equipment list requirements for alternate procedures are inadequate for cabin fire situations.
Inadequate guidance for pilots on donning oxygen masks and smoke goggles immediately.
Pilots did not don or delayed donning oxygen masks and smoke goggles.
Smoke goggle equipment requires excessive time and effort to don.
Sealed plastic wrapping on smoke goggles poses a potential hazard.
Emergency cockpit vision devices might have potential safety benefits.
Emerging technology might improve passenger respiratory protection.
Douglas smoke evacuation procedures would likely not have affected the outcome due to rapid fire propagation.
Oxygen generators should be actuated before transport.
Work card 0069 did not require an inspector’s signoff, potentially missing the lack of safety caps.
Work card 0069 lacked instructions for expending and disposing of generators.
Use of the wrong parts tag was a failure but probably did not contribute to the mishandling.
Maintenance duty time limitations may not be consistent with scientific knowledge on fatigue.
Air carrier maintenance programs do not adequately reflect human factors issues.
ValuJet’s practices might have included shipment of hazardous items aboard company airplanes.
Procedures for handling hazardous company materials are not fully consistent with regulations.
Employees need thorough training on handling hazardous materials.
ValuJet failed to implement training for subcontractor employees on hazardous materials authority.
